<section id="overview" class="content-section">

## What is Edwin Najmi Submission Attack System?

**The Edwin Najmi Submission Attack System is a BJJGraph study guide for recognising Darce, triangle and Estima-lock opportunities within distinct positional exchanges.**

Mission Submission groups Edwin Najmi's instruction into Darce, triangle and Estima-lock sections. The listed setups span top and bottom positions, with gi-dependent guard entries alongside techniques that do not require fabric grips. This makes the course a set of specialised attacking tracks rather than one universal chain.

BJJGraph's original plan below starts with the Darce track and adds a second family only when it fits the student's existing positions. The useful question is whether an opportunity appears during movement and can be converted into recognisable control. Submission-oriented study still needs positional judgement; a possible grip is not a reason to abandon a stable position or force an unfamiliar finish.

</section>

<section id="key-principles" class="content-section">

## Core Principles
- Choose one submission family before combining the course tracks.
- Recognise the positional opening before committing to the attacking grip.
- Keep gi-dependent setups separate from no-gi practice choices.
- Compare a top and bottom entry by the control available afterward.
- Treat Estima-lock control as a separate advanced study topic.
- Use grounded triangle entries before considering more dynamic variations.


</section>

<section id="key-components" class="content-section">

## Key Components
**Darce entry contexts** (Give the first study track a concrete positional focus.)
Compare a side-control entry with a half-guard entry and identify the head-and-arm relationship each requires.

**Triangle setup selection** (Match the chosen entry to the equipment and game being practised.)
Select a familiar grounded guard entry and note whether sleeve grips or other fabric controls are part of the setup.

**Estima-lock opportunity recognition** (Separate spotting the opportunity from executing an advanced lock.)
Study where the foot becomes accessible in a selected passing exchange without attempting a surprise application.

**Attack-or-position decision** (Keep the attacking objective connected to positional consequences.)
Assess whether pursuing the chosen submission preserves control or makes a pass, reversal or escape easier for the partner.



</section>

<section id="implementation-sequence" class="content-section">

## Implementation Sequence
1. **Begin with the Darce track**: Study one top side-control setup and end practice at a recognisable head-and-arm control position.


2. **Compare the half-guard context**: Use the matching half-guard lesson to identify what changes in access, available space and balance.


3. **Add one grounded triangle**: Choose a closed-guard or other familiar grounded entry. Note which grips are essential before trying it without the gi.


4. **Study an Estima entry separately**: With a coach, use one leg-drag context to identify the offered foot and a clear catch-and-release endpoint. Do not combine it with an uncontrolled passing round.


5. **Evaluate the attacking choice**: In a short positional exchange, name the attack that appeared and the position that would be surrendered to pursue it. Reset if the tradeoff is unclear.




</section>

<section id="common-obstacles" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## What Challenges Will You Face?
- **The three submission tracks become a disconnected move list.**: Start with the family that already appears in your rounds and delay the others.
- **A gi setup is attempted after removing its essential grip.**: Record fabric dependence and select a different demonstrated entry when appropriate.
- **The attacker abandons a useful pass for a loose submission grip.**: Compare the likely positional result with the control actually available.
- **An advanced foot-lock attempt surprises the partner.**: Use a separate coached recognition drill with an agreed catch-and-release endpoint.


</section>

<section id="assessment-metrics" class="content-section">

## How to Measure Your Progress
**Darce entry comparison**: Describe what differs between the chosen side-control and half-guard starts.
Proficiency indicators:
- Names the starting position
- Identifies head-and-arm access
- Recognises lost balance


**Grip-context fit**: Check whether the selected triangle setup fits the practice context.
Proficiency indicators:
- Identifies fabric grips
- Chooses a grounded entry
- Can explain a missing grip


**Foot-opportunity recognition**: Review recognition of the selected Estima-lock entry without pressure.
Proficiency indicators:
- Names the passing context
- Identifies the offered foot
- Uses the agreed endpoint


**Positional judgement**: Assess the cost of pursuing an attack during movement.
Proficiency indicators:
- Identifies the current position
- Describes the tradeoff
- Can decline an unsupported attack




</section>

<section id="training-methodology" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## How to Train This System Effectively

### Drilling Approach
BJJGraph suggests two separate Darce entry rounds: one from side control and one from half guard. Stop at head-and-arm control and compare the available space. Add a grounded triangle track later. Keep Estima-lock recognition in a separate coached catch-and-release exercise so the opportunity can be discussed without a surprise joint-lock application.

### Progression Path
**Darce access** (Focus: Recognise one side-control entry without finishing pressure.)
**Context comparison** (Focus: Study how half guard changes the same head-and-arm task.)
**Second family** (Focus: Choose one grounded triangle that fits the available grips.)
**Selective integration** (Focus: Recognise a submission opportunity and evaluate its positional cost.)


### Common Mistakes
- Trying to connect every course technique into one chain.
- Ignoring the fabric grips used by a selected guard entry.
- Confusing spotting an Estima-lock opportunity with readiness to apply it.


</section>
